newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan Taleban militia sets tough peace terms.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban militia sets tough peace terms.

text.p: Afghanistan's Taleban Islamic militia, reporting more victories north of Kabul, said on Saturday that opposition groups must accept it as the country's government as a condition for peace talks and a ceasefire.

"We are not against peace, and the opposition should accept the rule of the Islamic State of Afghanistan for there to be any kind of talks or ceasefire and (accept) that the restoration of tranquility be based on Islamic principles," the head of the Taleban government in Kabul, Mullah Mohammad Rabbani, told reporters.

Rabbani, head of the Taleban interim council in Kabul, was referring to what the militia calls a caretaker government that would give way to a government formed of all Afghanistan's warring factions after peace talks.

The Taleban-controlled Kabul radio said the militia on Friday took the districts of Shinwar and Siahgard, southwest of Ghorband district captured last week. About 2,000 opposition fighters defecting to the Taleban side, it added.

No country has formally recognised the Taleban government and frequent attempts by the United Nations, Pakistan and now Iran have so far failed to bring reconciliation between the Taleban and the government they drove from Kabul last September.
Leaders of the former government were in Tehran on Saturday for peace talks hosted by the Iranian government, but no Taleban delegation was present.
Rabbani said this was because the Iranian invitation to attend did not arrive in time.
"These talks will not have any result and nobody from Taleban has gone to Tehran because the invitation came late yesterday," he said.
Relations between mainly Shi'ite Iran and the mostly ethnic Pashtun Sunni Moslem Taleban, which controls most of a country devastated by 18 years of war, have been strained.
Tehran recognises the ousted government of Burhanuddin Rabbani -- no relation to Mullah Rabbani.

A spokesman for a Shi'ite Afghan group allied with the ousted government said on Saturday his Hezb-i-Wahdat party, led by Karim Khalili, had also declined an invitation to attend the Tehran talks, a Pakistan-based Afghan news service said.

The Afghan Islamic Press quoted the spokesman, Mohammad Rasul Talib, as saying in the northwestern Pakistani town of Peshawar that Wahdat wanted the peace talks to be held within Afghanistan under U.N. auspices, with Taleban also attending.

The Taleban are fighting forces of the deposed government's ethnic Tajik military chief Ahmad Shah Massoud and his ally, Uzbek leader Abdul Rashid Dostum, 110 km (70 miles) north of Kabul near the Hindu Kush mountains, where the population is mostly Tajik.
Thousands of people fled the area as the Taleban moved back in over the past few days, some saying they had been told to leave by the black-turbanned Taleban fighters.

However, Rabbani described allegations of ethnic cleansing as enemy propaganda. "It is all baseless that we are forcing the locals to vacate these areas. We know the ones who rose against us. Their number is very limited and we have told them to leave temporarily," he said.
